item.title: Lemala Kuria Hills Reimagines the Safari Stay in Tanzania’s Northern Serengeti
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Lemala Kuria Hills Lodge in Tanzania’s Northern Serengeti has completed a renovation designed to enhance the guest experience without expanding beyond its established wilderness footprint. The refresh introduces a new two-bedroom family suite with generous living space and a private plunge pool, relocates the spa and redesigns and expands the main dining tent. Set among the granite boulders and kopjes of Wogakuria Hill near the Mara River, the lodge remains ideally positioned for the Great Migration while offering year-round wildlife viewing.

The new family suite adds flexibility for multigenerational travelers and groups, while the redesigned dining and spa spaces strengthen the lodge’s connection to its surrounding landscape. Guests can also explore the Northern Serengeti by guided game drive, walking safari or hot-air balloon, with the region’s relatively low visitor density offering a more intimate wilderness experience.

The Curated Take: The renovation is notable for what it does not do. Rather than adding more structures to the landscape, Lemala has reworked its existing footprint to create a more flexible, family-friendly experience while preserving the sense of place that makes a remote Serengeti camp special. For travelers seeking safari with both comfort and a lighter touch on the wilderness, that distinction matters.

Photo credit: Lemala Camps and Lodges

item.title: At Patina Maldives, Guests Help Turn Art Into Part of the Reef
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
At Patina Maldives, Fari Islands, art is taking a decidedly underwater direction. Through September 12, 2026, the resort is hosting designer and artist Sean Wotherspoon for a collaboration spanning fashion, vintage design and marine conservation, culminating in Respect the Reef, a large-scale ceramic fish sculpture created with resort guests and now submerged in the lagoon as part of Patina’s ongoing coral restoration efforts.

The project brings Wotherspoon’s signature use of color into Patina’s existing ceramic coral workshops. Guests created and glazed individual ceramic scales, which were assembled onto a sculptural fish rather than the geometric structures traditionally used in the resort’s reef program. The completed work has now been placed underwater, where coral can attach and grow across its surface. Above water, Wotherspoon’s creative influence continues through an exclusive capsule collection of original artworks, vintage finds and reworked one-of-one pieces, including Hawaiian shirts and Carhartt shorts, displayed at the Fari Art Atelier.

The Curated Take

The most interesting luxury souvenirs are often the ones that don’t come home with you. At Patina Maldives, guests contribute to something that will remain long after their departure, watching a colorful piece of collaborative art gradually become part of the marine environment. It’s a particularly compelling expression of experiential luxury: the memory is personal, but the creation ultimately belongs to the reef.

Photo Credit: Patina Maldives, Fari Islands

item.title: Hamilton Island Wins Travel Brand of the Year in Australia
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Hamilton Island has been named Travel Brand of the Year – Destination at the 2026 Mumbrella Travel Marketing Awards, recognizing the Australian island’s evolving brand, marketing strategy and creative work. The award follows a period of significant investment, including the debut of The Sundays boutique hotel, a refreshed dining scene featuring Catseye Pool Club by Josh and Julie Niland, and updates to longtime island favorites. In August 2025, Hamilton Island also launched A Little Island Can Do Wonders, its first major brand campaign since 2017, inviting travelers to rediscover the Whitsundays destination.

At the heart of the island’s latest chapter is a broader evolution of the guest experience, from its 20 restaurants and extensive activities to its access to Whitehaven Beach and the Great Barrier Reef. With 70 percent of the island protected, Hamilton Island combines resort amenities with opportunities to explore the surrounding landscape, while recent accolades for properties including qualia and The Sundays add to its growing international profile.

The Curated Take: The award is less about a single campaign than what Hamilton Island has built around it. The destination is using new hospitality, dining and experiences to give travelers a fresh reason to return, while its latest branding connects that evolution back to the simple appeal of an island escape. It is a useful reminder that a strong destination brand has to keep giving travelers something new to discover.

Photo credit: Hamilton Island

item.title: Scottsdale’s Culinary Scene Earns Five Michelin Guide Southwest Honors
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Scottsdale is making a notable showing in the inaugural MICHELIN Guide Southwest, with five restaurants recognized in the guide’s first selection covering Arizona, Nevada, New Mexico and Utah. FnB earned a Bib Gourmand for chef Charleen Badman’s seasonally driven celebration of Arizona farmers and producers, while Hush Public House, Indibar, Reserve and Shinbay received Michelin Recommended honors. Reserve’s wine director, John Germain, also received a Sommelier Award, while Badman was recognized with a Mindful Voices Award for her work advancing sustainability and food access through the Blue Watermelon Project.

The selection follows Michelin’s expansion into the Southwest and its evaluation of restaurants based on quality of ingredients, harmony of flavors, cooking technique, culinary personality and consistency. For travelers, the recognition puts Scottsdale’s increasingly diverse dining scene firmly on the culinary map, highlighting everything from Arizona-focused cooking and Indian cuisine to Japanese omakase and sophisticated wine programs.

The Curated Take: Michelin’s inaugural Southwest guide gives travelers another reason to put Scottsdale on the itinerary. More importantly, the range of honors shows a destination dining scene that goes well beyond resort restaurants, with local ingredients, global influences and chefs who are putting their own stamp on the Southwest.

Photo credit: Experience Scottsdale and Jill Richards Photography

item.title: Coastal Mississippi’s Fall Calendar Turns Milestones Into Reasons to Visit
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
From live blues and songwriter sessions to classic cars, catamaran racing, art festivals and Gulf Coast seafood, Coastal Mississippi is heading into fall with a calendar that is as diverse as its 62 miles of shoreline. Beginning Labor Day weekend and continuing through November, the destination’s biggest events combine long-running local traditions with milestone celebrations that give travelers plenty of reasons to plan a coastal escape.

The season begins with the 7th Annual Booker Fest in Bay St. Louis and Artwalk Downtown Ocean Springs over Labor Day weekend, followed by the Biloxi Box Set Music Festival, Biloxi Seafood Festival and 35th Annual Gulf Coast Blues Festival. September also brings the Hobie 16 International Championship, drawing top catamaran sailors from around the world, and the Mississippi Songwriters Festival, where roughly 200 singer-songwriters will perform across Ocean Springs and Gautier. Later in the month, Banana Ball brings its deliberately unpredictable brand of baseball to Biloxi.

October shifts the spotlight to one of Coastal Mississippi’s biggest traditions, as Cruisin’ the Coast celebrates its 30th anniversary with more than 10,000 classic, antique and hot rod vehicles traveling along Highway 90. The fall calendar continues with the 40th Annual Fall Muster, the 10th Annual Gulf Coast Equality Fest and the century-plus Jackson County Blue Ribbon Fair. November brings the 48th annual Peter Anderson Arts & Crafts Festival in Ocean Springs, followed by Bud & Burgers in the Bay and the Scottish Highland Games and Celtic Music Festival.

The Curated Take: The appeal of Coastal Mississippi in fall isn’t simply that there is something happening every weekend. It’s that the events reveal the character of the destination. Music reflects its Southern and Gulf Coast roots, Cruisin’ the Coast turns the shoreline into a moving celebration, art festivals showcase local creativity, and sailing puts the region’s waterways center stage. For travelers, the calendar offers an easy reason to choose a particular weekend and then build a broader coastal getaway around it.

Photo credit: Coastal Mississippi / Visit Mississippi

item.title: Sonoma County Is Collecting the Kind of Accolades That Influence Travel Plans
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Sonoma County is having a particularly strong year on the awards circuit, with recognition arriving across museums, wine, restaurants and hotel bars.

The Charles M. Schulz Museum and the Children’s Museum of Sonoma County were named among the San Francisco Chronicle’s Top 10 Bay Area Museums. Domaine de la Rivière’s 2021 Ritchie Vineyard Chardonnay was included in Robb Report’s 50 Greatest California Chardonnays of the 21st Century, while Mascarin Family Wines landed on the San Francisco Chronicle’s list of Top Wineries in Sonoma County for 2026. At Graton Resort & Casino, AYA earned Wine Spectator’s Best of Award of Excellence for its wine program only two months after opening.

The recognition extends into hospitality, too. Andys Beeline Rooftop at Appellation Healdsburg was named the No. 4 hotel bar in the United States in USA TODAY 10Best’s 2026 Readers’ Choice Awards. Together, the honors paint a picture of a destination whose appeal is increasingly broad, from cultural institutions and serious wine to restaurants and places to linger over a drink.

The Curated Take: Awards don’t necessarily make a destination worth visiting, but they can be useful signposts when deciding where to spend limited vacation time. What’s notable about Sonoma County’s latest collection is its breadth. The recognition isn’t concentrated in one category. It touches the experiences travelers increasingly use to define a destination: what they eat, drink, see and where they stay.

item.title: The Mother Road, Redefined
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
For nearly a century, Route 66 has been encoded in the global imagination as a singular, unyielding myth. We know the cultural shorthand by heart: neon-drenched motels blinking against the twilight, chrome-laden tailfins, roadside pie, and endless ribbons of two-lane asphalt stretching across 2,400 miles of North American terra incognita. It is a journey traditionally defined by endurance—a relentless, cross-country drag race designed to be swallowed whole from the shores of Lake Michigan to the Pacific surf of Santa Monica.

Yet, in our modern era of hyper-connected, fast-paced travel, the classic 14-day highway grind feels less like a getaway and more like an exercise in fatigue.

The secret to discovering the true magic of Route 66 today lies in a quiet reinterpretation: you do not need to take the highway as it was given to you.

Long before the Mother Road became a gallery of pop-culture kitsch, it was an artery of transformation. When paved in 1926, it didn’t merely connect small towns; it linked distinct geographic ecosystems, architectural movements, and native foodways across eight states and three time zones. The road was drawn across landscapes that had long For nearly a century, Route 66 has been defined by the myth of the 2,400-mile cross-country grind. But in an era of fast-paced travel, the traditional 14-day highway rush feels less like an escape and more like an exercise in fatigue.

The true magic of the Mother Road lies in quiet reinterpretation: choosing quality of place over quantity of miles. By stripping away roadside novelties and focusing on world-class sanctuaries, architectural icons, and regional foodways, Route 66 becomes an intentional, luxury getaway. Here is how to experience America’s main street through three curated lenses.

Lens 1: The High-Desert Reset

Spas, Thermal Mineral Waters & Alpine Sanctuaries

Reclaiming the West’s history as a place for the “climate cure,” this 8-day itinerary trades long driving marathons for multi-night wellness anchors across New Mexico and Arizona. Move intentionally from the high-alpine ponderosa pines of Santa Fe down into the red-rock canyons of Sedona and the geothermal hot springs of the Sonoran Desert. Read the complete interactive feature

Lens 2: The Design & Architecture Trail

Midwestern Art Deco, Prairie Style & River City Masonry

Stretching from Chicago across the Illinois prairie to St. Louis, the upper corridor of Route 66 serves as an open-air museum of modern American architecture. This 5-day journey explores the roots of the skyscraper, Frank Lloyd Wright’s organic Prairie Style masterpieces, historic capital masonry, and monumental riverfront engineering. Read the complete interactive feature

Lens 3: The Epicurean Highway

High-Plains Ranchlands, Native Harvests & Southwestern Spirits

Bypass tourist steakhouses for a 5-day culinary exploration of native foodways, cattle trails, and high-plains terroir. Tracing the path from Oklahoma City across the Texas Panhandle to Albuquerque, this itinerary pairs private heritage ranch visits and botanical gin distilleries with farm-to-table dining at historic agricultural estates. item.title: Cowboy Core Has Found Its Range in Sonoma County
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Cowboy Core may be having a moment on fashion feeds, but in Sonoma County, the trend has considerably deeper roots. Ranching, horseback riding, Western wear and country music have long been part of the region’s culture. Now they’re becoming part of the travel experience, too.

In Windsor, Spur Saloon has opened as a country-western bar and live music venue with dancing, line dancing and karaoke. Grapevine Dance is bringing country line-dancing lessons to venues around the county, including the historic Washoe House and Twin Oaks Roadhouse. At Lake Sonoma, The Ranch at Lake Sonoma offers guided horseback rides through the 17,000-acre recreation area, with routes overlooking the lake, Dry Creek Valley and Rockpile wine region, including experiences that pair a ride with a picnic and local wine or beer.

The look can come home with you, too. Santa Rosa’s The Hattery is a working hat factory, showroom and museum specializing in Western hats and bespoke designs, while Blanton’s Boot & Hat in downtown Petaluma offers premium cowboy boots, custom hats, leather goods and Western apparel. On Sonoma Plaza, Large Leather has been crafting fine leather goods for more than 45 years, including belts with Western-style buckles, while Bosworth & Son General Merchandise in Geyserville has been selling Western wear since 1911. The historic mercantile remains a multigenerational family business and offers custom hat shaping, cleaning and restoration.

The Curated Take: This is where a social trend meets an authentic sense of place. Sonoma County doesn’t have to manufacture a cowboy aesthetic for visitors. It already has the ranches, horses, craftsmen, historic mercantiles and country music to support it. For travelers, that means Cowboy Core can be more than a pair of boots for the weekend. It can become a way of experiencing the region.

Photo credit: The Hattery

item.title: Four New Ways to Experience Sonoma County Beyond the Tasting Room
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Wine may remain central to Sonoma County’s identity, but some of the destination’s newest experiences are looking elsewhere, toward food, agriculture, art and the redwoods.

In downtown Petaluma, Taste Petaluma brings four local concepts together under one roof: Barber Cellars, Petaluma Cheese Shop, Barber Lee Spirits and Nightcap Dessert Bar. Guests can move from Sonoma County wines and craft cocktails to artisan cheeses, chocolates and desserts in a relaxed lounge setting. In Santa Rosa, Gold Ridge Organic Farms is opening Heritage Apple Press, a 20,000-square-foot facility designed to process fruit from small and family-owned farms, helping preserve the region’s apple-growing heritage while supporting fresh-packed apples, juice, cider and vinegar.

Art is also becoming part of the resort experience. Fairmont Sonoma Mission Inn & Spa has debuted the Lori Austin Gallery at the Fairmont, a rotating pop-up gallery showcasing contemporary work by regional artists. And for travelers who would rather head into the trees, Sonoma Zipline Adventures is expanding with Redwood Aerial Adventure, a 40,000-square-foot ropes and challenge course expected to open in spring 2027, with aerial routes, sky bridges and a separate treetop play area for younger visitors.

The Curated Take: The appeal here is variety. Sonoma County can still be a wine destination, but travelers increasingly want something to do between tastings, whether that means discovering local producers, seeing regional art or climbing into a redwood canopy. These experiences give visitors more reasons to slow down and engage with the place itself.

item.title: Six New Restaurants Are Giving Sonoma County Even More Reasons to Stay for Dinner
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Sonoma County’s culinary scene is having another busy season, with new restaurants and cafés adding everything from charcoal-grilled Northern California cooking to handmade pasta, East Coast bagels and Chinese-inspired food.

On Sonoma Plaza, the team behind the girl & the fig has opened Dead Letter in a historic former post office, where seasonal seafood, meats and vegetables share the menu with a globally minded wine list and postal-inspired cocktails. In Santa Rosa, Capriciano Osteria brings chef-owner Baki Bekci’s fine-dining background to a neighborhood-style Italian restaurant centered on handmade pasta, wood-fired pizza and Sonoma County ingredients. Meanwhile, Mei Mei is planned for Healdsburg, giving Sean Quan and Jenny Phan, the team behind Bazaar Sonoma, a new home for their Chinese-style food hall and grocery concept after their Forestville restaurant was lost in a 2025 fire.

West Sonoma County is also getting a new community gathering place with Graton Station, a café and bakery taking over the town’s former firehouse. In Sebastopol, Bonnie Bagels & Co. is bringing kettle-boiled, East Coast-style bagels to downtown, while Dolce Rosa Café in Santa Rosa’s Rincon Valley combines brunch, Italian-inspired dishes and specialty espresso drinks, with pistachio making an especially prominent appearance across the menu.

The Curated Take: The most interesting thing about Sonoma’s restaurant boom isn’t simply the number of openings. It’s the range of stories behind them. Chefs are bringing fine-dining experience into neighborhood spaces, couples are rebuilding after loss, historic buildings are finding new lives and longtime local businesses are creating gathering places. The result is a food scene that feels increasingly woven into the communities travelers come to explore.
